new_statements.quote: The word is a distinct phonological entity in Rengao and may be summarized as: PW = #(S)S# [p. 121] That is, a weakly stressed preliminary syllable (S) may optionally occur preceding the more strongly stressed main syllable (S). Word boundaries # are defined as the interval directly following the first of two successive (not necessarily contiguous) S's.

new_statements.rule_in_words: The Rengao phonological word is sesquisyllabic: an optional weakly stressed 'preliminary syllable' (presyllable, typically two segments, with a non-contrastive vowel) followed by the obligatory, more strongly stressed main syllable. Stress therefore falls on the main syllable, which is always the last (and in monosyllables the only) syllable of the word; the presyllable is never the stronger syllable. Gregerson uses the strong/weak stress contrast itself to define the word boundary (the boundary falls right after each main syllable). In the scanned both syllable symbols appear as 'S'; the print distinguishes them with diacritics that the scanned lost.
new_statements.secondary_stress: None as such; the presyllable is characterised only as 'weakly stressed' relative to the main syllable. No statement on longer or compound words.
new_statements.exceptions: None in the fragments retrieved (searches inside the book for 'stress', 'intonation', 'pitch', 'monosyllabic', 'disyllabic' return no further hits; only 'stressed' occurs, in this passage).
new_statements.domain_note: Phonological word (PW), citation-level description in a grammar appendix; nothing on phrase-level prominence. Gregerson 1976 (open, read) adds that the presyllable vowel is non-contrastive and harmonises with the main-syllable vowel and register (Jadrap dialect), consistent with the weak-syllable status but with no stress statement of its own.
new_statements.identity_note: Gregerson 1979 describes Rengao of Kontum Province without naming a dialect in the fragments seen; the 1977 vocabulary's introduction distinguishes Central Rengao (principal dialect, west/north of Kontum City), Southeastern 'Bahnar-Rengao' (bahn1261) and Northern 'Sedang-Rengao' (seda1260); Glottolog also lists Western Rengao (west2400). Gregerson 1976 refers specifically to the 'Jadrap dialect' for vowel harmony. The stress statement should be taken as Central Rengao / language-level reng1252.

sources.note: The two-page 'Pronunciation' guide (pp. vii-viii, Rosetta Project scan) covers consonants (preglottalized, preaspirated, final glottal stop marked by breve) and the two vowel registers (lax vs tense), plus hyphen = syllable division; nothing on stress or accent. Only 4 of 178 pages are open; the full book is not online.

sources.citation: Gregerson, Kenneth J. 1976. Tongue-root and register in Mon-Khmer. In Philip N. Jenner, Laurence C. Thompson & Stanley Starosta (eds), Austroasiatic Studies, Part I, 323-369. Honolulu: University Press of Hawaii.
sources.note: Silent on Rengao stress. Register (tense/lax, tongue-root) phonology of Rengao; the only 'stressed/accented' mention is a quotation from Fromkin & Ohala about English F0 (scanned line 1397). Describes the Jadrap-dialect presyllable as 'Ca-' with a non-contrastive vowel determined by the main-syllable vowel and register (scanned lines 1550-1560) — sesquisyllabic structure, no explicit stress statement.
